Base64-encoded configuration values ​

Context ​

Configuration values travel through carriers that only hold a single line of text: environment variables, .env files, CI variable stores, container orchestrator manifests and secret managers. Some values do not fit. TLS certificates and CA bundles are multi-line PEM, and a Google service account key is a multi-line JSON document with an embedded PEM key. Each carrier mangles newlines, quotes and backslashes differently, so the same value pasted into two carriers can reach the program in two different shapes. This happens to public values and secrets alike.

Encoding the value as base64 makes it a single line of safe characters, but the program reading it has to know it was encoded. Putting that knowledge in the reader's configuration, such as an encoding field next to the variable name, does not travel: the operator who stores the value often cannot change the reader's configuration, and a value shared by programs in different languages would need the same field in every one of them. The value has to describe itself.

Other ecosystems already do this, such as the base64: prefix Laravel uses for APP_KEY.

ADR#3610135900 defines a syntax that marks a value as a secret so scanners can find it. This ADR does not replace it; it defines how a value is carried, not what it is.

Resolution ​

When to encode ​

Encoding is a last resort for a value its carrier cannot hold unchanged. It costs readability: people, diffs and scanners can no longer see what the value is.

  • You SHOULD NOT encode a value that already fits on one line of printable ASCII, such as a URL, an API token or a whsec_ signing secret.
  • You SHOULD NOT encode a value when the carrier already preserves it, such as a Kubernetes ConfigMap or Secret, which delivers the exact bytes to the program, or a secret manager that returns them unchanged. A Secret's data field is already base64, so encoding the value again only adds a layer.
  • You MAY encode a value only when its carrier cannot hold it unchanged, such as a multi-line PEM certificate in a .env file or a CI store that strips newlines.

Writing a value ​

  • You MUST write an encoded value as base64: followed by the standard base64 encoding of the value's bytes, as defined in RFC 4648 section 4, with padding:

    txt
    base64:LS0tLS1CRUdJTiBDRVJUSUZJQ0FURS0tLS0tCk1JSUIKLS0tLS1FTkQgQ0VSVElGSUNBVEUtLS0tLQo=

  • You MUST encode a text value as its UTF-8 bytes.

  • You MUST NOT change the bytes before encoding, such as by normalizing newlines or trimming whitespace, so the decoded value is the original one.

  • You MUST write the prefix in lowercase.

  • You SHOULD write the encoded part as a single line, such as the output of base64 -w0 or of base64 on macOS.

  • You MUST encode a value that itself begins with base64:, so it is not mistaken for an encoded one.

  • You MUST NOT use the URL-safe alphabet or drop the padding.

Reading a value ​

  • You MUST decode a value that begins with base64: and use the decoded value in its place.
  • You MUST use a value that does not begin with base64: as is. You MUST NOT guess an encoding from the content of a value.
  • You MUST decode exactly once. A decoded value that begins with base64: is the value itself, not another layer to decode.
  • You MUST ignore ASCII whitespace inside the encoded part, so wrapped output of base64 is accepted. Base64 contains no whitespace, so this cannot change the result.
  • You MUST fail when the encoded part is not valid standard base64. When the reader needs text, it MUST also fail when the decoded bytes are not valid UTF-8.
  • You SHOULD decode when the configuration is loaded and fail at startup, not each time the value is used.

Encoding a secret ​

The ADR#3610135900 marker is what tells scanners, logs and people that a value is sensitive. Encoding hides the content, so the marker has to stay readable.

  • You MUST mark every encoded secret with the ADR#3610135900 syntax, so scanners detect it without decoding it.

  • You MUST keep the marker outside the encoding: put base64: at the start of the secret value part, after the namespace identifiers.

    txt
    secret:tls:private-key:base64:LS0tLS1CRUdJTiBQUklWQVRFIEtFWS0tLS0tCk1JSUUKLS0tLS1FTkQgUFJJVkFURSBLRVktLS0tLQo=

  • You MUST NOT encode a marked value as a whole, such as base64:c2VjcmV0Oi4uLg==, since that hides the marker.

  • When reading, you MUST parse the ADR#3610135900 syntax first, then apply Reading a value to its secret value part.

  • You MUST NOT include a secret, encoded or decoded, in an error or a log. Name where the value came from instead, such as the variable or field.
